clue.text: Aussie weed producing rubbish wickets (12, two words, apostrophe)

parts.note: cobblers is British slang for nonsense or rubbish
in cricket the stumps of a wicket are pegs driven into the ground

explanation.surface: A troublesome Australian weed turns a cricket pitch into a mess of poor wickets.
explanation.walkthrough: Cobblers is British slang for rubbish, and a cricket wicket's stumps are pegs.
explanation.definitionFit: Cobbler's pegs is the Australian common name for Bidens pilosa, a burr-seeded plant regarded as a garden pest there.

clue.text: N American plant clubs gather lots of

parts.note: amass means to gather in large quantity

explanation.surface: Groups gather plenty of a North American plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Camass is a North American plant of the lily family whose bulbs were eaten by Native Americans.

clue.text: Stay-at-home nerds fazed out about even parts of walk

indicators.note: about means the jumbled letters go round the others
fazed means the letters of out are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: even parts means the second and fourth letters of the word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Home-loving geeks are flustered by stepping out, managing only part of a walk.
explanation.definitionFit: Otaku is a Japanese term for obsessive fans who rarely leave home, used in English for geeky enthusiasts.

clue.text: Fungal growth endured after taking in silly oasis dip

indicators.note: after taking in means the word for endured contains the jumbled letters

parts.note: bore means endured

indicators.note: silly means the letters are arranged foolishly in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Mould appeared after someone took a foolish plunge in a desert pool.
explanation.definitionFit: A basidiospore is a spore produced by club fungi such as mushrooms, the means by which they reproduce.

clue.text: Rib cooked pastry confection, home-grown creative effort

indicators.note: cooked means the letters are doctored into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
a tart is a pastry case with filling

explanation.surface: A cooked rib and a tart make a homemade creation.
explanation.walkthrough: Home-grown means British: Britart was the 1990s movement of Young British Artists.
explanation.definitionFit: Britart names the art produced by British artists, notably the Young British Artists of the 1990s.

clue.text: French demanding leave to import European cherry (wild)

indicators.note: to import means the exit word takes the cherry inside it

parts.note: exit means to leave
the gean is the wild cherry of Europe

explanation.surface: A fussy French visitor insists on leaving to bring in wild cherries.
explanation.definitionFit: Exigeant is the French adjective for demanding or exacting, used in English for a hard-to-please person.

clue.text: Covering for icon surfaced in US Academy

parts.note: riz is an American dialect past tense of rise

explanation.surface: A cover for an icon turned up at an American academy.
explanation.walkthrough: Riz, for rose, is US dialect.
explanation.definitionFit: A riza is the metal plate covering an Orthodox icon, leaving only faces and hands visible.

clue.text: Feature of pretty decoration suspended from earlobe?

definitions.text: Feature of pretty decoration suspended from earlobe?

indicators.note: feature of picks out the opening letter, the most prominent part of the word

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: suspended from means the decoration's letters are taken away from the word

parts.note: taken as written
the OBE is a British honour, Officer of the Order of the British Empire

explanation.surface: A pretty ornament dangles from the lobe of an ear.
explanation.walkthrough: The OBE is a British honour; removing it from earlobe leaves the earl.
explanation.definitionFit: A pearl drop is a classic earring hanging from the lobe, so the whole clue describes the gem.

clue.text: Re bloodstain, I'm worried — such clotting Dr treated

definitions.text: Re bloodstain, I'm worried — such clotting Dr treated

indicators.note: treated says the doctor's letters are part of the jumble too, so they are set aside from the shuffled pool

parts.note: worried means these letters are tugged into a new order, giving the answer plus the doctor's letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: A patient frets over a bloodstain caused by clotting a doctor brought about.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a composite anagram: the answer plus DR together rearrange to make the opening words.
explanation.definitionFit: Embolisation is a medical procedure in which a doctor deliberately blocks a blood vessel, often by inducing a clot.

clue.text: 'Ivy'-flavoured beer giving you wind, sick inside (7, two words)

indicators.note: inside means the sick word sits within the wind word

parts.note: a gale is a strong wind
ill means sick

explanation.surface: A herbal beer gives the drinker wind and a queasy stomach.
explanation.definitionFit: Gill ale was beer flavoured with gill, or ground ivy, used before hops became common.

clue.text: Calm, almost pivotal when a sailor's leading

indicators.note: the sailor's piece goes in front of the rest

parts.note: taken as written
a tar is a sailor

indicators.note: almost means the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: axial means forming an axis, the pivot something turns on

explanation.surface: Someone stays almost unflappable when a seaman takes charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Ataraxia is a philosophical term for serene tranquillity, freedom from anxiety.

clue.text: Producer topped and tailed Spenserian tale

indicators.note: topped and tailed means the first and last letters are cut off

parts.note: a breeder produces animals or plants

explanation.surface: A producer trims the start and finish of a story from Spenser.
explanation.definitionFit: Reede is Spenser's spelling of rede, meaning counsel or a tale told.

clue.text: Pretty big maize given little breadth in bucket

indicators.note: in places the maize and breadth pieces inside the word for bucketing down

parts.note: sile is a dialect verb meaning to pour with rain, as does bucket
Zea is the botanical genus of maize
a little breadth is its abbreviation B

explanation.surface: A sizeable heap of corn is crammed into a pail with little room to spare.
explanation.walkthrough: Bucket here is the verb, to rain hard, which the Scots and dialect word sile also means.
explanation.definitionFit: Sizeable means fairly large, so pretty big is a close paraphrase.

clue.text: Big dog: it's protected by alias

indicators.note: protected by means surrounded by the alias letters

parts.note: aka, also known as, introduces an alias
the word it, with the s of is serving as a link

explanation.surface: A large dog has been given a false name for its own protection.
explanation.definitionFit: The Akita is a large Japanese breed of spitz-type dog.

clue.text: Working-class p-part

parts.note: taken as written
a role is a part in a play

explanation.surface: A stammered word for a part played by the working class.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphenated p-part reads like a stutter but asks for the letter P followed by a word for part.
explanation.definitionFit: Prole is informal for a member of the proletariat, and is used adjectivally for working-class.

clue.text: Sweat rarely, as young fellow back in court once

indicators.note: in puts the reversed word inside the archaic word for courting

parts.note: sue was formerly used to mean woo or court

indicators.note: back means the young fellow's word is read from the end

parts.note: tad is American for a small boy

explanation.surface: A youngster rarely breaks a sweat when returning to a former court.
explanation.walkthrough: Rarely flags that the answer is a rare word, and once that sue in the courting sense is obsolete.
explanation.definitionFit: Sudate is a rare verb meaning to perspire, from Latin sudare.

clue.text: Old lettuce, etc — everything inside quite droopy

indicators.note: inside means the word for everything goes within the other piece

parts.note: sad can describe something limp and heavy, such as wilted leaves or bread that has not risen
all means everything

explanation.surface: Some old lettuce has gone thoroughly limp all the way through.
explanation.definitionFit: Sallad is an obsolete spelling of salad, a dish of lettuce and other greens.

clue.text: What makes sling for lance?

parts.note: read as a recipe, the word sling is built from a single letter joined by and to the name of a fish; lance is the fish called the sand lance, not a weapon

explanation.walkthrough: Spelt out, the answer is S and LING, which does make sling; lance is the fish, not a weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandling is another name for the sand eel, also called the sand lance.

clue.text: I tucked into Nimble, becoming thinner?

indicators.note: tucked into means the letter goes inside the word for nimble

parts.note: spry means nimble and active
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone eating a Nimble loaf, a slimming bread, asks whether they will get slimmer.
explanation.walkthrough: Nimble was a British brand of light bread sold as a slimming aid, hence the capital and the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Spiry means tapering like a spire, narrowing to a point as it rises.

clue.text: Old fold: kid missing I'd found involved in gambolling?

indicators.note: found involved in means the remaining letter sits inside the capering word

parts.note: prance means to caper or gambol

indicators.note: missing means the letters I and D are dropped from the word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An old sheepfold where a young goat was found frisking about.
explanation.walkthrough: Fold is the verb, to pleat, not a sheep pen.
explanation.definitionFit: Prancke is Spenser's spelling of prank in its obsolete sense of to pleat or arrange in folds.

clue.text: Alcoholic stuff destroyed lei, once alight

parts.note: ava, or kava, is an intoxicating Polynesian drink

indicators.note: destroyed means the letters of the garland are wrecked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Strong drink ruined a garland that was once burning.
explanation.walkthrough: Alight is not on fire here but the verb, to come down or dismount.
explanation.definitionFit: Availe is a Spenserian form of avale, to descend or dismount, which is what alight means as a verb.

clue.text: Heavenly tree having trouble with insect, old

parts.note: ail means to trouble
the ant is an insect

explanation.surface: A celestial tree is plagued by an old insect problem.
explanation.definitionFit: Ailanto is a form of ailanthus, the tree of heaven.

clue.text: Tropical plant to put amid wild corn

indicators.note: put amid means placed in the middle of the scrambled letters
wild means the letters of corn run riot into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grower places a tropical specimen among a field of wild corn.
explanation.definitionFit: Croton is a genus of tropical shrubs, and the name is also given to the ornamental codiaeum houseplant.

clue.text: Will no longer in Church employment

parts.note: use means employment, putting something to work

explanation.surface: A will is no longer held in the employment of the Church.
explanation.walkthrough: Will is the verb, to choose, not a legal document.
explanation.definitionFit: Chuse is an obsolete spelling of choose, and to will is to choose or decide.

clue.text: Optional extra in old chippie maybe is surrounded by fish

definitions.text: Optional extra in old chippie maybe

indicators.note: surrounded by means the word is goes inside the fish

parts.note: the eel is a fish
taken as written

explanation.surface: An extra on the menu of an old fish shop comes wrapped in fish.
explanation.walkthrough: A chippie is a fish-and-chip shop, where vinegar is the extra you may add; eisel is the Shakespearean word for vinegar.
explanation.definitionFit: Eisel is an archaic word for vinegar, the condiment customers may choose to sprinkle on chips.

clue.text: What monkeys get up to put one in school punishment!

indicators.note: put tells you the one is being placed somewhere
in says where: inside the punishment word

parts.note: lines are sentences a pupil must copy out as punishment
a means one

explanation.surface: Monkeys' antics earn them lines as a school punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: Get up to suggests mischief, but it means climb.
explanation.definitionFit: Lianes, or lianas, are the woody climbing vines that monkeys clamber up in forests.

clue.text: Tolerates permitted offal

parts.note: has, as in will not have it, means tolerates
let means permitted

explanation.surface: Someone puts up with offal that has been allowed on the menu.
explanation.definitionFit: Haslet is a British meatloaf made from pig's offal such as liver and heart.

clue.text: Pleasant record kept inside cover

indicators.note: kept inside means the record sits within the cover

parts.note: a lid is a cover
an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A nice record is stored inside its sleeve.
explanation.definitionFit: Lepid is a rare word for pleasant or charming, from Latin lepidus.

clue.text: Some African brass regrettably impounded by senior policeman

indicators.note: impounded by means held within the policeman's letters

parts.note: DI is a Detective Inspector
alas is said regretfully

explanation.surface: Some brass from Africa has sadly been seized by a high-ranking officer.
explanation.walkthrough: Brass is British slang for money, so the definition is a currency.
explanation.definitionFit: The dalasi is the currency of the Gambia in West Africa, and brass is slang for cash.

clue.text: Rarely controlled son getting out of last piece of work?

indicators.note: getting out of means the son's letters are removed

parts.note: a swan song is a final work or performance
taken as written

explanation.surface: A seldom-disciplined son quits before finishing his final task.
explanation.walkthrough: Swang is a rare past tense of swing, which can mean to control or sway an outcome.
explanation.definitionFit: To swing something, such as a vote or deal, is to influence or control it, and swang is its rare past form.

clue.text: Take down gym slips among what's 'oisted aloft?

indicators.note: slips among means the gym letters slide inside the other piece

parts.note: hung is what is hoisted aloft, spoken with its h dropped as the apostrophe shows
PE, physical education, is the school gym lesson

explanation.surface: Someone in a Cockney voice orders the gym slips taken off the line they were hung on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oisted mimics a dropped h, which tells the solver to drop the h of hung too.
explanation.definitionFit: To unpeg is to unfasten from a peg, so taking down washing or a tent.

clue.text: Stoppage once central to James Joyce originally?

indicators.note: central to reads as one instruction; to completes it, so the closing letters of the title are shed as well
central means only the middle of the title is wanted, so its opening letters are shed

parts.note: Joyce's first prose book was the story collection Dubliners

explanation.surface: A puzzle about what once stood at the heart of the writer James Joyce.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a loose hidden word: the letters lie at the centre of Dubliners, the title of Joyce's early book, not in the clue itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Blin is a Spenserian word meaning cessation or a halt, now obsolete.

clue.text: Death sentence following fighting (not right)

parts.note: f is the abbreviation for following, as in page references

indicators.note: not right means the letter for right is removed

parts.note: at war means fighting

explanation.surface: A sentence of death is handed down after a battle in which someone was in the wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: A fatwa is a ruling by an Islamic authority, best known in the West for one that called for a writer's death.

clue.text: Spotted fish? Catch sight of moving eye cover

parts.note: scope means to look at or view
a lid is the movable cover of the eye

explanation.surface: An angler spots a fish and glimpses a flickering eyelid.
explanation.walkthrough: Spotted looks like the past of spot, but it describes a fish dotted with light organs.
explanation.definitionFit: Scopelids are lanternfishes, whose bodies are dotted with luminous spots called photophores.

clue.text: Inert, nog drunk? I can go off just about anywhere!

definitions.text: I can go off just about anywhere!

indicators.note: drunk means the letters are reeling into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sluggish drinker boasts of being able to drop off to sleep anywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Go off suggests falling asleep; here it means sounding, as a phone does.
explanation.definitionFit: A ringtone is the sound a mobile phone makes when called, and it may sound in almost any place.

clue.text: We'll go to work in bed, no good fashion in tiny accommodation

definitions.text: We'll go to work in bed

parts.note: wee means tiny

indicators.note: in places the no-good and fashion letters inside the tiny lodgings

parts.note: digs are lodgings
the ton is the prevailing fashion

explanation.surface: Workers say they'll do their job from bed, in a cramped flat that is hopelessly unfashionable.
explanation.walkthrough: Bed is a flower bed, not a place to sleep; digs is British for rented rooms.
explanation.definitionFit: Weeding tongs are a gardening tool used to pull weeds out of a flower bed.
